title: HashMap resize internals: power-of-two, hash & (capacity-1), oldIndex + oldCapacity redistribution
keyPoints: Resize triggers when size exceeds capacity times load factor (default: 12 entries for capacity 16 with load factor 0.75)
Capacity always doubles to the next power of 2 (16 to 32 to 64 to 128), enabling fast bitwise bucket indexing
Bucket index is hash & (capacity - 1), equivalent to hash % capacity but using bitwise AND which is ~10x faster than modulo
Java 8 optimizes redistribution: each entry either stays at its current index or moves to oldIndex + oldCapacity, decided by checking one bit
The one-bit check: hash & oldCapacity; if 0, entry stays; if 1, entry moves to oldIndex + oldCapacity
Resize is O(n) because every entry is visited; pre-sizing avoids this cost for known data volumes
Load factor 0.75 balances space efficiency (higher wastes less) and lookup speed (lower has fewer collisions)

s1_definition.oneliner: HashMap resizes by doubling capacity (always power-of-2) and redistributing entries using a one-bit check: hash & oldCapacity determines if an entry stays at its index or moves to index + oldCapacity.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Trigger**: resize when `size > capacity * loadFactor` (default threshold = 16 * 0.75 = 12)
- **New capacity**: doubles the old capacity (16 → 32 → 64); always a power of 2
- **Bucket index**: `hash & (capacity - 1)` – bitwise AND is ~10x faster than modulo; power-of-2 capacity makes this work
- **Java 8 redistribution**: for each entry, check `hash & oldCapacity`; if 0, stay at current index; if 1, move to `oldIndex + oldCapacity`
- **Cost**: O(n) – every entry is visited and potentially moved
- **Pre-sizing**: `new HashMap<>(expectedSize * 4/3 + 1)` avoids resize entirely
s1_definition.analogy: A filing cabinet has 16 drawers. When 12 drawers are used (75%), buy a cabinet with 32 drawers (double). Moving files: each file either stays in its current drawer or moves to drawer currentDrawer + 16. This is determined by looking at one extra bit in the file's code – no need to recalculate the full drawer assignment from scratch. Why powers of 2? Because `hash & 15` (for 16 drawers) is one CPU instruction, much faster than `hash % 16` which requires division.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Resize: capacity 16 → 32

  Old mask: 0b01111 (15)      New mask: 0b11111 (31)
  Extra bit:         ^ (bit 4 = 16 = oldCapacity)

  For each entry in bucket 3:
    hash & 16 == 0?  → stays at index 3
    hash & 16 != 0?  → moves to index 3 + 16 = 19

  Before resize (16 buckets):
  [0] [1] [2] [3:A,B,C] [4] ... [15]

  After resize (32 buckets):
  [0] [1] [2] [3:A,C] [4] ... [15] [16] [17] [18] [19:B] [20] ... [31]
              lo chain                              hi chain

  Pre-sizing formula:
  capacity = expectedSize / 0.75 + 1
  HashMap rounds up to next power of 2
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
HashMap resize is triggered when the number of entries exceeds capacity times load factor. Capacity always doubles to the next power of 2, enabling the fast bitwise AND trick for bucket indexing: `hash & (capacity - 1)` instead of the slower `hash % capacity`.

Java 8 made resize smarter. Instead of rehashing every entry, it checks one bit: `hash & oldCapacity`. If that bit is 0, the entry stays at its current index. If 1, it moves to oldIndex + oldCapacity. This splits each bucket into exactly two groups with a single bit operation per entry.

In the National Bank of India's account cache, Rajesh pre-sizes the HashMap to avoid resize during the EOD batch load of 2 million records. Without pre-sizing, the map resizes about 20 times, each time copying millions of entries to a new table. With `new HashMap<>(2_700_000)`, the map allocates enough capacity upfront and never resizes.

Remember one sentence: HashMap doubles its power-of-2 capacity at 75% load, and Java 8 redistributes entries with a single-bit check instead of full rehashing.
